concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (Cramer's rule)
questions.question:
Consider the system of equations $x-2y+3z=-1$, $-x+y-2z=k$, $x-3y+4z=1$.
STATEMENT-1: The system of equations has no solution for $k\neq3$.
and
STATEMENT-2: The determinant $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 3 & -1 \\ -1 & -2 & k \\ 1 & 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\neq 0$, for $k\neq3$.   [JEE-2008]
options: Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is True; Statement-2 is NOT a correct explanation for Statement-1
Statement-1 is True, Statement-2 is False
Statement-1 is False, Statement-2 is True
questions.key_idea: If $\Delta=0$, the system is inconsistent exactly when one of $\Delta_x,\Delta_y,\Delta_z$ is non-zero.
solution: Take the coefficient determinant of the system: $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}$.
Expanding along the first row: $\Delta=1(4-6)+2(-4+2)+3(3-1)=-2-4+6=0$.

Since $\Delta=0$, the system has either no solution or infinitely many solutions; this is decided by $\Delta_x,\Delta_y,\Delta_z$ (the determinants with the constants column $-1,k,1$ put in place of a column).
The determinant in Statement-2 has columns (coefficients of $x$), (coefficients of $z$), (constants). Expanding it: $1(-2-4k)-3(-1-k)-1(-4+2)=-2-4k+3+3k+2=3-k$.
So Statement-2 is true: the determinant equals $3-k$, which is non-zero for $k\neq3$.
This determinant is $\Delta_y$ up to a sign (swapping the last two columns gives $\Delta_y=k-3$).
For $k\neq3$: $\Delta=0$ but $\Delta_y\neq0$, so the system has no solution; Statement-1 is true.
For $k=3$ all the determinants vanish and the system has infinitely many solutions (e.g. $x=-z-5,\ y=z-2$).
Statement-2 ($\Delta_y\neq0$ for $k\neq3$) is exactly the reason for the inconsistency in Statement-1, so it is a correct explanation. Option (A).

alternate_solutions.idea: Find the linear dependency among the left-hand sides; the right-hand sides must obey the same dependency.
solution: Add the first two equations: $(x-2y+3z)+(-x+y-2z)=-y+z=-1+k$.
Subtract the first equation from the third: $(x-3y+4z)-(x-2y+3z)=-y+z=1-(-1)=2$.
Both left sides equal $-y+z$, so the system is consistent only if $k-1=2$, i.e. $k=3$.
Hence for $k\neq3$ the system has no solution (Statement-1 true); for $k=3$ it reduces to two independent equations with infinitely many solutions.
Statement-2: expanding the determinant gives $3-k\neq0$ for $k\neq3$, true, and it is the $\Delta_y$ non-vanishing that signals inconsistency when $\Delta=0$. Option (A).

useful_results: For a $3\times3$ system with $\Delta=0$: if some $\Delta_x,\Delta_y,\Delta_z\neq0$, there is no solution; if all vanish the system may still be inconsistent (e.g. parallel planes), so check the rows.

If $\text{row}_3=\lambda\,\text{row}_1+\mu\,\text{row}_2$ in the coefficients, the system is consistent iff the constants satisfy $c_3=\lambda c_1+\mu c_2$. Here $\text{row}_3=2\,\text{row}_1+\text{row}_2$, so $1=2(-1)+k$ gives $k=3$.
In Assertion-Reason questions on systems, test the reason by computing it, not by recognising the shape of the determinant.

concepts: Solution of a system of linear equations
questions.question:
The number of all possible values of $\theta$, where $0<\theta<\pi$, for which the system of equations
$(y+z)\cos3\theta=(xyz)\sin3\theta$
$x\sin3\theta=\frac{2\cos3\theta}{y}+\frac{2\sin3\theta}{z}$
$(xyz)\sin3\theta=(y+2z)\cos3\theta+y\sin3\theta$
have a solution $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ with $y_0z_0\neq0$, is.   [JEE-2010]
questions.key_idea: Eliminate $xyz\sin3\theta$ between the equations to get $y+z=0$, $x=0$, then $\tan3\theta=1$.
solution: Label the equations: (i) $(y+z)\cos3\theta=xyz\sin3\theta$, (ii) $x\sin3\theta=\frac{2\cos3\theta}{y}+\frac{2\sin3\theta}{z}$, (iii) $xyz\sin3\theta=(y+2z)\cos3\theta+y\sin3\theta$, with $yz\neq0$ and $0<\theta<\pi$.
From (i) and (iii): $(y+z)\cos3\theta=(y+2z)\cos3\theta+y\sin3\theta$, so $z\cos3\theta+y\sin3\theta=0$ ... (iv).
Multiply (ii) by $yz$: $2z\cos3\theta+2y\sin3\theta=xyz\sin3\theta$ ... (v).
By (iv), the left side of (v) is $2(z\cos3\theta+y\sin3\theta)=0$, so $xyz\sin3\theta=0$.
Since $yz\neq0$, this gives $x\sin3\theta=0$: either $x=0$ or $\sin3\theta=0$.
Case 1, $x=0$: (i) gives $(y+z)\cos3\theta=0$. Taking $y+z=0$, i.e. $y=-z$, equation (iv) becomes $\cos3\theta=\sin3\theta$, i.e. $\tan3\theta=1$.

For $0<\theta<\pi$ we have $0<3\theta<3\pi$, so $3\theta=\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4},\frac{9\pi}{4}$, i.e. $\theta=\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{9\pi}{12}$. Check: with $x=0$, $y=-z$ each of (i), (ii), (iii) holds.
Case 2, $\sin3\theta=0$: then $\theta=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\cos3\theta=\pm1$; (iv) gives $z\cos3\theta=0$, so $z=0$, contradicting $yz\neq0$. These values are rejected.
Hence the total number of possible values of $\theta$ is $3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $P=xyz\sin3\theta$ and combine (ii)$\times yz$ with (iii) first: the unknowns cancel to give $\tan3\theta=1$ at once, with no case split.
solution: Let $c=\cos3\theta$, $s=\sin3\theta$, $P=xyz\,s$. Then (i): $(y+z)c=P$; (iii): $P=(y+2z)c+ys$; (ii)$\times yz$: $P=2zc+2ys$.
Equate (iii) and (ii)$\times yz$: $(y+2z)c+ys=2zc+2ys$, so $yc=ys$.
Since $y\neq0$, $c=s$, i.e. $\cos3\theta=\sin3\theta$. Both cannot vanish together, so $c=s\neq0$.
Equate (i) and (ii)$\times yz$: $(y+z)c=2zc+2yc$ (using $s=c$), so $(y+z)c=2(y+z)c$, hence $(y+z)c=0$ and $y+z=0$ because $c\neq0$.
Then $P=(y+z)c=0$; as $yz\neq0$ and $s=c\neq0$, $x=0$. So the solution is $(0,y,-y)$, and it exists exactly when $\tan3\theta=1$.
For $0<\theta<\pi$: $3\theta\in(0,3\pi)$ and $\tan\phi=1$ has three roots there ($\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{4},\frac{9\pi}{4}$). Answer $3$, same as before.

useful_results: The number of solutions of $\tan\phi=c$ in $(0,m\pi)$ is exactly $m$ (one per period); with $\phi=3\theta$ and $0<\theta<\pi$, $m=3$.
When equations contain a common expression such as $xyz\sin3\theta$, treat it as one unknown $P$ and eliminate it; the system collapses to a few linear relations.
A candidate with $\sin3\theta=0$ (or $\cos3\theta=0$) should be tested separately: here it forces $z=0$ and is rejected.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Properties of determinants (row and column operations)
questions.question: Which of the following values of $\alpha$ satisfy the equation $\begin{vmatrix} (1+\alpha)^2 & (1+2\alpha)^2 & (1+3\alpha)^2 \\ (2+\alpha)^2 & (2+2\alpha)^2 & (2+3\alpha)^2 \\ (3+\alpha)^2 & (3+2\alpha)^2 & (3+3\alpha)^2 \end{vmatrix}=-648\alpha$?   [JEE-Adv.-2015]
questions.key_idea: Differences of consecutive squares are linear, so row and column differences reduce the determinant to a triangular shape.
solution: Apply $R_3\to R_3-R_2$ and $R_2\to R_2-R_1$. Row 2 becomes $(3+2\alpha,\ 3+4\alpha,\ 3+6\alpha)$ and row 3 becomes $(5+2\alpha,\ 5+4\alpha,\ 5+6\alpha)$.
Apply $R_3\to R_3-R_2$ again: row 3 becomes $(2,\ 2,\ 2)$.

Apply $C_3\to C_3-C_2$ and $C_2\to C_2-C_1$. Row 1 becomes $\left((1+\alpha)^2,\ \alpha(2+3\alpha),\ \alpha(2+5\alpha)\right)$, row 2 becomes $(3+2\alpha,\ 2\alpha,\ 2\alpha)$, row 3 becomes $(2,\ 0,\ 0)$.
Expand along row 3 (only the entry $2$ in column 1 is non-zero, with sign $+$): $2\left[\alpha(2+3\alpha)\cdot2\alpha-\alpha(2+5\alpha)\cdot2\alpha\right]=-648\alpha$.
Dividing by 2: $2\alpha^2(2+3\alpha)-2\alpha^2(2+5\alpha)=-324\alpha$.
Simplify: $2\alpha^2(-2\alpha)=-4\alpha^3=-324\alpha$, so $\alpha(\alpha^2-81)=0$.
Therefore $\alpha=0,\ 9,\ -9$. Of the options, $9$ and $-9$ are listed; $-4$ and $4$ are not roots. Options (B) and (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: The entry $(i+j\alpha)^2=i^2\cdot1+2i\cdot j\alpha+1\cdot j^2\alpha^2$ makes the matrix a product of two $3\times3$ Vandermonde-type matrices.
solution: Expand each entry: $(i+j\alpha)^2=i^2\cdot1+(2i)(j\alpha)+1\cdot(j\alpha)^2$.
Hence the matrix is $U\,W$ with $U$ having rows $(i^2,\ 2i,\ 1)$ for $i=1,2,3$, and $W$ having columns $(1,\ j\alpha,\ j^2\alpha^2)^T$ for $j=1,2,3$.
$\det U=2\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\4&2&1\\9&3&1\end{matrix}\right|=2(-2)=-4$.
$\det W=\alpha\cdot\alpha^2\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\1&2&3\\1&4&9\end{matrix}\right|=\alpha^3\cdot2=2\alpha^3$ (scale rows by $1,\alpha,\alpha^2$ first).
So the determinant is $(-4)(2\alpha^3)=-8\alpha^3$, and $-8\alpha^3=-648\alpha$ gives $\alpha(\alpha^2-81)=0$.
$\alpha=0,\pm9$; options (B) $9$ and (C) $-9$. Same answer.

useful_results: For any $x_i,y_j$: $\det\left[(x_i+y_j)^2\right]_{3\times3}=-2\,(x_1-x_2)(x_2-x_3)(x_3-x_1)\,(y_1-y_2)(y_2-y_3)(y_3-y_1)$. Here $x=1,2,3$ and $y=\alpha,2\alpha,3\alpha$ give $-8\alpha^3$.
Entries that are squares of linear terms form a matrix of rank at most 3 (product of two $3\times3$ matrices); an $n\times n$ determinant of $(x_i+y_j)^2$ is $0$ for $n\ge4$.
First differences of squares of an arithmetic sequence are linear and second differences are constant: use consecutive row differences to create a constant row.

concepts: Properties of determinants (splitting a column, Vandermonde form)
questions.question: The total number of distinct $x\in\mathbb{R}$ for which $\begin{vmatrix} x & x^2 & 1+x^3 \\ 2x & 4x^2 & 1+8x^3 \\ 3x & 9x^2 & 1+27x^3 \end{vmatrix}=10$ is.   [JEE-Adv.-2016]
questions.key_idea: Split the third column as $1+x^3$-terms; both parts are Vandermonde-type and equal $2x^3$ and $12x^6$.
solution: Split the third column: the determinant equals $D_1+D_2$ with $D_1=\left|\begin{matrix}x&x^2&1\\2x&4x^2&1\\3x&9x^2&1\end{matrix}\right|$ and $D_2=\left|\begin{matrix}x&x^2&x^3\\2x&4x^2&8x^3\\3x&9x^2&27x^3\end{matrix}\right|$.
Use the identity $\left|\begin{matrix}a&a^2&1\\b&b^2&1\\c&c^2&1\end{matrix}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$ with $a=x$, $b=2x$, $c=3x$.

In $D_2$ take $x,2x,3x$ out of the three rows: $D_2=(x)(2x)(3x)\left|\begin{matrix}1&x&x^2\\1&2x&4x^2\\1&3x&9x^2\end{matrix}\right|=6x^3\left|\begin{matrix}1&x&x^2\\1&2x&4x^2\\1&3x&9x^2\end{matrix}\right|$.
Moving the column of ones to the end is a cyclic change of columns (an even permutation), so this determinant is again $(x-2x)(2x-3x)(3x-x)=2x^3$.
Hence $D_2=6x^3\cdot2x^3=12x^6$, and the equation becomes $2x^3+12x^6=10$, i.e. $2x^3(1+6x^3)=10$.
Each real $t$ gives exactly one real $x$: $x=\left(\frac56\right)^{1/3}$ and $x=-1$.
The number of distinct real values of $x$ is $2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Plain row reduction: subtract multiples of $R_1$ from $R_2,R_3$ to clear the first column; no Vandermonde lemma is needed.
solution: Apply $R_2\to R_2-2R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-3R_1$ on the original determinant.
Expand along column 1: determinant $=x\left[2x^2(24x^3-2)-6x^2(6x^3-1)\right]=x\cdot x^2\left[48x^3-4-36x^3+6\right]=x^3(12x^3+2)$.
So $2x^3(6x^3+1)=10$, the same equation as before; solving gives $x^3=-1$ or $\frac56$ and 2 real values of $x$.

useful_results: For any $a,b,c$: $\left|\begin{matrix}a&a^2&1+a^3\\b&b^2&1+b^3\\c&c^2&1+c^3\end{matrix}\right|=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\,(1+abc)$ (verified symbolically).
A determinant of rows $(a,a^2,1)$ or $(1,a,a^2)$ is the Vandermonde value $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$; moving the column of ones around is a cyclic (even) permutation, so no sign change.
With arithmetic-progression rows ($x,2x,3x$) the Vandermonde factor is $2x^3$; an equation in $x^3$ only is a quadratic in $t=x^3$, and every real $t$ gives exactly one real $x$.

questions.type_label: One or more than one Correct Type
concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations (Cramer's rule)
questions.question: Let $a,\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb{R}$. Consider the system of linear equations $ax+2y=\lambda$, $3x-2y=\mu$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?   [JEE-Adv.-2016]
options: If $a=-3$, then the system has infinitely many solutions for all values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$
If $a\neq-3$, then the system has a unique solution for all values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$
If $\lambda+\mu=0$, then the system has infinitely many solutions for $a=-3$
If $\lambda+\mu\neq0$, then the system has no solution for $a=-3$
questions.key_idea: Compare the ratios $\frac a3$, $\frac{2}{-2}$, $\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$ to decide unique, infinite or no solution.
solution: For the system $a_1x+b_1y=c_1$, $a_2x+b_2y=c_2$: a unique solution exists when $\frac{a_1}{a_2}\neq\frac{b_1}{b_2}$, i.e. here $\frac a3\neq\frac{2}{-2}$.
Infinitely many solutions when $\frac a3=\frac{2}{-2}=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$.
No solution when $\frac a3=\frac{2}{-2}\neq\frac{\lambda}{\mu}$.
Here $\frac{2}{-2}=-1$, so $\frac a3=-1$ means $a=-3$.
(A) For $a=-3$ the system has infinitely many solutions only if $\frac\lambda\mu=-1$, i.e. $\lambda+\mu=0$; for other $\lambda,\mu$ there is no solution. So (A) is false.
(B) For $a\neq-3$ the ratios $\frac a3$ and $-1$ differ, so the solution is unique for all $\lambda,\mu$. (B) is true.
(C) For $a=-3$ and $\lambda+\mu=0$: $\frac\lambda\mu=-1=\frac a3$, so the two equations coincide and there are infinitely many solutions. (C) is true.
(D) For $a=-3$ and $\lambda+\mu\neq0$: $\frac\lambda\mu\neq-1$, so the system has no solution. (D) is true. Answer (B, C, D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Add the two equations: $y$ cancels, leaving $(a+3)x=\lambda+\mu$.
solution: Adding $ax+2y=\lambda$ and $3x-2y=\mu$ gives $(a+3)x=\lambda+\mu$.
If $a\neq-3$: $x=\frac{\lambda+\mu}{a+3}$, and then $y=\frac{3x-\mu}{2}$ is determined. Unique solution for every $\lambda,\mu$: (B) true.
If $a=-3$ the sum equation is $0=\lambda+\mu$. If $\lambda+\mu\neq0$ it is impossible, so no solution: (D) true, and (A) is false.
If $a=-3$ and $\lambda+\mu=0$ the first equation $-3x+2y=\lambda$ is the same as $3x-2y=-\lambda=\mu$, the second equation: one line, infinitely many solutions, (C) true.
Answer (B, C, D), same as before.

useful_results: For $a_1x+b_1y=c_1$, $a_2x+b_2y=c_2$ with $\Delta=a_1b_2-a_2b_1$: $\Delta\neq0$ unique; $\Delta=0$ gives infinitely many solutions if the constants follow the same ratio, otherwise none.
Adding or subtracting the equations to cancel one variable shows directly which single condition ($a+3=0$, and then $\lambda+\mu=0$) controls the outcome.
A question with 'for all values of ...' needs a check at the exceptional parameter value, not only the generic case.

questions.question:
Let $p,q,r$ be nonzero real numbers that are, respectively, the $10^{th}$, $100^{th}$ and $1000^{th}$ terms of a harmonic progression. Consider the system of linear equations $x+y+z=1$, $10x+100y+1000z=0$, $qr\,x+pr\,y+pq\,z=0$.
List-I: (I) If $\frac qr=10$, then the system has; (II) If $\frac pr\neq100$, then the system has; (III) If $\frac pq\neq10$, then the system has; (IV) If $\frac pq=10$, then the system has.
List-II: (P) $x=0,\ y=\frac{10}{9},\ z=-\frac19$ as a solution; (Q) $x=\frac{10}{9},\ y=-\frac19,\ z=0$ as a solution; (R) infinitely many solutions; (S) no solution; (T) at least one solution.
The correct option is:   [JEE(Adv.)2022]
questions.key_idea: Reciprocals of an HP are in AP, and the third equation is $(a-d)\times$(first) $+\ d\times$(second) in its left side.
solution: Equation (3) divided by $pqr$ reads $\frac xp+\frac yq+\frac zr=0$ (since $p,q,r\neq0$).
$p,q,r$ are in HP, so $\frac1p,\frac1q,\frac1r$ are in AP: let $\frac1p=a+9d$, $\frac1q=a+99d$, $\frac1r=a+999d$.
Equation (3) becomes $(a+9d)x+(a+99d)y+(a+999d)z=0$.
The coefficient determinant is $\Delta=\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\10&100&1000\\a+9d&a+99d&a+999d\end{matrix}\right|=0$.
$\Delta_x=\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\0&100&1000\\0&a+99d&a+999d\end{matrix}\right|=900(d-a)$.
$\Delta_y=\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\10&0&1000\\a+9d&0&a+999d\end{matrix}\right|=990(a-d)$.
$\Delta_z=\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\10&100&0\\a+9d&a+99d&0\end{matrix}\right|=90(d-a)$.
Conditions: $\frac qr=\frac{a+999d}{a+99d}=10\iff a=d$; $\frac pr=\frac{a+999d}{a+9d}=100\iff a=d$; $\frac pq=\frac{a+99d}{a+9d}=10\iff a=d$.

(I) $\frac qr=10\Rightarrow a=d$, so $\Delta=\Delta_x=\Delta_y=\Delta_z=0$. Equations (1), (2) are non-parallel planes and (3) is a multiple of (2): infinitely many solutions. So (I) $\to$ P, Q, R, T.

(II) $ rac pr
eq100\Rightarrow a
eq d$: $\Delta=0$ but $\Delta_x,\Delta_y,\Delta_z
eq0$, so there is no solution: (II) $	o$ S.
(III) $\frac pq\neq10\Rightarrow a\neq d$: no solution: (III) $\to$ S.
(IV) $\frac pq=10\Rightarrow a=d$: infinitely many solutions, so (IV) $\to$ P, Q, R, T.
The option consistent with all four is (B): (I)$\to$(Q), (II)$\to$(S), (III)$\to$(S), (IV)$\to$(R); (A), (C), (D) each assign (R) or (P) to a no-solution case.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write equation (3) as $(a-d)(x+y+z)+d(10x+100y+1000z)$; the first two equations then fix its left side to the number $a-d$.
solution: With $\frac1p=a+9d$ etc., the coefficients of (3) are $a+9d=(a-d)\cdot1+d\cdot10$, $a+99d=(a-d)\cdot1+d\cdot100$, $a+999d=(a-d)\cdot1+d\cdot1000$.
So the left side of (3) is $(a-d)(x+y+z)+d(10x+100y+1000z)$.
Using (1) and (2) this equals $(a-d)\cdot1+d\cdot0=a-d$, but (3) says it is $0$: the system is consistent iff $a=d$.
If $a\neq d$ the system has no solution. If $a=d$, equation (3) is $d\times$(2), so only (1) and (2) remain: infinitely many solutions.

$ rac qr=10$, $ rac pq=10$ each force $a=d$ (infinite solutions); $ rac pr
eq100$ and $ rac pq
eq10$ force $a
eq d$ (no solution). (P) and (Q) satisfy (1), (2), hence (3) when $a=d$.
Matching gives option (B). Same answer.

useful_results: If $\text{row}_3=\lambda\,\text{row}_1+\mu\,\text{row}_2$ in the coefficients, then (3) is consistent with (1), (2) iff $c_3=\lambda c_1+\mu c_2$; otherwise no solution, and no determinant calculation is needed.
Reciprocals of terms of an HP form an AP, so $\frac1{p}$ at positions $10,100,1000$ is linear in the position: $a+9d,\ a+99d,\ a+999d$.
For $a=d$ every term of the AP is a multiple of the position: $\frac1p=10d$, $\frac1q=100d$, $\frac1r=1000d$ (so $q/r=10$, $p/q=10$, $p/r=100$ all hold together).

concepts: Consistency of a system of linear equations with parameters
questions.question:
Let $\alpha, eta,\gamma$ be real numbers. Consider the system of linear equations $x+2y+z=7$, $x+\alpha z=11$, $2x-3y+ eta z=\gamma$. Match each entry in List-I to the correct entries in List-II.
List-I: (P) If $ eta= rac12(7\alpha-3)$ and $\gamma=28$, then the system has; (Q) If $ eta= rac12(7\alpha-3)$ and $\gamma
eq28$, then the system has; (R) If $ eta
eq rac12(7\alpha-3)$ where $\alpha=1$ and $\gamma
eq28$, then the system has; (S) If $ eta
eq rac12(7\alpha-3)$ where $\alpha=1$ and $\gamma=28$, then the system has.
List-II: (1) a unique solution; (2) no solution; (3) infinitely many solutions; (4) $x=11$, $y=-2$ and $z=0$ as a solution; (5) $x=-15$, $y=4$ and $z=0$ as a solution.
The correct option is:   [JEE(Adv.)2023]
questions.key_idea: $D=7\alpha-2\beta-3$; when $D=0$ the sign of $\Delta_z=56-2\gamma$ decides, and $\alpha=1$ gives $y=-2$ at once.
solution: Coefficient determinant: $D=\left|\begin{matrix}1&2&1\\1&0&\alpha\\2&-3&\beta\end{matrix}\right|=1(3\alpha)-2(\beta-2\alpha)+1(-3)=7\alpha-2\beta-3$.
$D=0\iff\beta=\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}$.
With $\gamma=28$ and $\beta=\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}$: $D_x=\left|\begin{matrix}7&2&1\\11&0&\alpha\\28&-3&\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}\end{matrix}\right|=21\alpha-\left[11(7\alpha-3)-56\alpha\right]-33=0$.

Similarly $D_y=\left|\begin{matrix}1&7&1\\1&11&\alpha\\2&28&\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}\end{matrix}\right|$; with $R_1\to R_1-R_2$ this is $4\left[\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}-2\alpha\right]+(1-\alpha)(28-22)=14\alpha-6-8\alpha+6-6\alpha=0$.
$D_z=\left|\begin{matrix}1&2&7\\1&0&11\\2&-3&\gamma\end{matrix}\right|=33-2(\gamma-22)-21=56-2\gamma$, which is $0$ for $\gamma=28$.
(P) $\beta=\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}$, $\gamma=28$: $D=D_x=D_y=D_z=0$, infinitely many solutions: (P) $\to$ (3).
(Q) $\beta=\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}$, $\gamma\neq28$: $D=0$ but $D_z=56-2\gamma\neq0$, so no solution: (Q) $\to$ (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Eliminate $x$ and $y$ by substitution to reduce the system to a single equation $(2\beta-7\alpha+3)\,z=2(\gamma-28)$.
solution: From equation 2: $x=11-\alpha z$.
Equation 1: $11-\alpha z+2y+z=7$, so $y=\frac{(\alpha-1)z}{2}-2$.
Equation 3: $2(11-\alpha z)-3\left[\frac{(\alpha-1)z}{2}-2\right]+\beta z=\gamma$, i.e. $28+z\left(\beta-2\alpha-\frac{3(\alpha-1)}{2}\right)=\gamma$.
Multiplying by 2: $(2\beta-7\alpha+3)\,z=2(\gamma-28)$. The coefficient is $-D$.
If $2\beta-7\alpha+3=0$ ($\beta=\frac{7\alpha-3}{2}$): $\gamma=28$ gives $0\cdot z=0$, so infinitely many solutions (P)$\to$(3); $\gamma\neq28$ gives $0=2(\gamma-28)\neq0$, no solution (Q)$\to$(2).

If the coefficient is non-zero, $z=\frac{2(\gamma-28)}{2\beta-7\alpha+3}$: unique solution. For $\alpha=1$: $y=-2$ for every $z$, and $z=0\iff\gamma=28$. So (R) has $z\neq0$ and is just (1); (S) has $z=0$, $y=-2$, $x=11$, i.e. (4). Option (A).

useful_results: Eliminate two unknowns to reduce a parametric $3\times3$ system to a single equation $c\,z=\rho$: unique if $c\neq0$; infinite if $c=0=\rho$; none if $c=0\neq\rho$. Here $c=-D=2\beta-7\alpha+3$.
If $D=0$, test a single minor ($D_z=56-2\gamma$) for the condition under which the constants fit.
For $\alpha=1$, equations 1 and 2 give $2y=-4$: $y=-2$ is forced for every $\beta,\gamma$, which kills option (5).
